results.text:
Eben Sprinsock, where are you?

The capabilities of AI have just put me in a somewhat complicated ethical situation. 

Long long ago, in 1985, there was a DOS shareware game called Firefighter. It was a nifty little firefighting simulation in a virtual forest with changing winds, where each turn you could drop water or firebreaks in an attempt to stop the raging inferno before it incinerated houses scattered through the forest. 

Earlier this evening I found a copy of the DOS binary. It only took me a few minutes of work to decompile it, and then translate the recovered Borland Pascal to Rust using the crossterm library. Robot friend did a pretty good job of assigning sensible function and variable names; the resulting source is quite readable.

I'd like to publish this as an open source game, with a little adaptation. There would be no point in preserving the logic path for monochrome display at this point, and there's no need to assume the quite tiny display that was all Sprinsock's game could then count on having.

The legal situation is clear. Even though I've never seen Sprinsock's original code, my port of the decompiled binary would be a derivative work, and a potential copyright violation. 

The ethical situation is less clear. The game was distributed as shareware, which meant it was allowed to be freely redistributed, with a request for donation attached. But it is extremely unlikely that there is still any revenue stream attached to it, as the entire  ecology of DOS shareware collapsed a good 30 years ago now.

Furthermore, it appears that the game was based on a real-time firefighting simulation built into a arcade-game cabinet in Canada sometime before 1980. There are some online recollections from people who played that game and connected it with Sprinsock's game from 5 years later.

It seems to me this changes the ethical situation a bit. Sprinsock's game wasn't quite an original creation, it was a folk-process adaptation of the original video game. If it was okay for him to do that, it's arguably okay for me to folk-process it again, with due credit to both him and the original videogame.

Still, I'd like to find the guy if I can to get permission. I think I found his YouTube channel - appears he's a lighting designer who's been involved with the Brothers Karamazov, a neo-vaudeville  act his members actually knew slightly decades ago when they were getting their start performing at science-fiction conventions. But I can't find an email address for him and there doesn't seem to be any way to DM him. 

Oh hivemind, please help! Does anybody know him? Is he still alive? (Born in 1953, according to one bio page I found.) How can I reach this guy?

(Robot friend won't help me turn up an email address. Says it would be a privacy violation. Hmmmmph.)

Here's a typical gherkin file. 

Scenario Outline: file operations normalize file paths
  Given filename input is <filename>
  And environment variable SPRINGDIR is <springdir>
  When the coder resolves an XSP filename
  Then resolved filename should be <resolved_filename>

Examples:
  | filename | springdir | resolved_filename        |
  | demo     | unset     | demo.xsp                 |
  | demo.xsp | unset     | demo.xsp                 |
  | demo     | examples  | examples/demo.xsp        |

I like to use the Examples format because it make it easier to mutate the gherkin.

results.text: There is no point in mutation testing a function that has not been changed since its last mutation test. So I have the tool create a manifest in a comment at the end of each module. The manifest contains an entry for each function in the module. The entry for a function contains a hash code for the function, and other things like the date of the last mutation, etc. This allows differential mutation testing. The tester will hash each function, and compare the hashes to the manifest. Only those functions whose hash codes don’t match are mutated. This can save a ton of computer and clock time.

I get how uncomfortable it feels to disengage from the syntax, from the sequence, selection, and iteration of code, from the dopamine hit of getting a complicated function to execute properly.  I get it.  I've been coding for longer than most of you have been alive -- I get it.

But the bar has been raised.  And if I, someone who has been coding for more than six decades, can clear that bar, you should be able to clear it too.  

And fear not, I've found plenty of joy on the topside of that bar.  It just take a leap...

results.text:
Why gherkin?
Gherkin scenarios are composed of three elements. Given, when, then. These three elements are precisely, the same elements in every finite state machine transition.

Given that the machine is in state X, when the machine receives event Y, then the machine goes to state Z.

What this means is that gherkin is a language for specifying finite state machines. And every computer program ever written is a finite state machine. Finite state machines are Turing complete.  Therefore gherkin is a sufficient language for specifying any software system.

Having said that, gherkin may not be the best way to express things like wire frames, aesthetics, and the typical creative artwork of graphical user interfaces.

results.text:
I've been allowing the swarm to operate for a full day now.  It's gotten a lot done.  But I've intentionally allowed the agents to continue compacting their contexts, over and over.  

The results are interesting.  First, they've started to lose their particular identities.  The coders is doing crap analysis.  The refactorer finds it has nothing to do because the coder did it.  The refactorer has decided that sending message to other agents requires my permission (it doesn't).  The coder simply forgets to hand off to the refactorer until I remind it.  The architect decided to not run mutation tests because they take a long time.   

Fascinating.  

Given all that, and the constant babysitting that is required, it has gotten a LOT done.  

As the number of testing scenarios has increased, the testing procedures have gotten quite slow.  The continual retesting is very inefficient.  I'm going to have to implement impact analysis to drive the tests so that only the things that have changed are tested.

results.text:
I'm having my swarm code up the old xspringies app from the early 90s.  The specifier broke things up into over 22 tasks, and then specified each in Gherkin.  The coder, refactorer, and architect are eating through the pipeline, building acceptance tests, unit tests, and production code.  The code is being analyzed for CRAP, and coverage.  The architect runs mutation testing, dry testing, and acceptance mutation.  

They've been working for three hours now, and are about half done.  There were a few hiccups.  Sometimes the agents stall because they lose track of what they are doing.  I have to remind them.  That usually takes no more than we typing: "What should you be doing right now?"  They're like lazy little kids.
